metadata.summary: These guidelines address spinal cord stimulation for chronic pain, covering candidate selection, preparation, implantation, follow-up, rehabilitation, and complication management. They also discuss stimulation targets and modes, practitioner training, multidisciplinary care, and service quality. Deep brain stimulation and sacral nerve stimulation are outside the guideline’s stated scope.

conditions_covered: mechanical and nociceptive axial low back pain
postsurgical pain with neuropathic and nociceptive pain
target_population: patients with chronic, refractory pain unresponsive to standard medical therapies
appropriately selected patients with refractory neuropathic or mixed pain despite comprehensive multidisciplinary management
patients undergoing SCS trials or permanent implantation
patients with focal neuropathic pain considered for DRG stimulation
therapeutic_areas: restorative neuromuscular electrical stimulation (L2 medial branch)

therapies_index.name: SCS
approved_indications: Chronic refractory neuropathic or mixed pain when comprehensive multidisciplinary care has not provided adequate pain relief or functional improvement
PSPS
Localized CRPS
PDN, as an emerging option
Critical limb ischemia, with primarily observational evidence
Refractory angina in selected cases after other treatments have failed
Pelvic and visceral pain, including interstitial cystitis, as emerging indications requiring careful selection and auditing
therapies_index.administration: A screening trial generally precedes permanent implantation. The recommended trial lasts five to seven days; a suitable patient may be considered for implantation without a trial under the specified implanter-experience criteria.
key_toxicities: Dural breach and cerebrospinal fluid leak
Hardware malfunction, battery failure, rare allergic reactions, and lead adhesions
Declining stimulation effectiveness or altered pain perception over time
monitoring: During a trial, maintain daily contact and assess pain relief, function, quality of life, and activities of daily living.
Inspect wounds and assess device performance, neurologic symptoms, infection, bleeding, and lead migration.
Arrange an initial wound review within 1–2 wk; programming reviews are suggested at 2–4 wk, 3 mo, 6 mo, and 12 mo, with further visits as needed.

therapies_index.name: cervical SCS
approved_indications: Cervical radicular pain
Upper extremity CRPS
Cervical axial pain
PSPS (cervical)
therapies_index.administration: The advised lead position is between C2 and C6, with epidural entry at C7–T4 or T11–L1 and placement guided by imaging and anatomical considerations.
monitoring: Intraoperative neuromonitoring is recommended when difficult cervical lead placement is anticipated.

therapies_index.name: Tonic SCS
therapies_index.mechanism: Stimulation at 30–120 Hz produces paresthesia in the stimulated regions.
approved_indications: A broad range of neuropathic pain

therapies_index.name: High-frequency SCS
therapies_index.mechanism: Paresthesia-free stimulation involves dorsal horn inhibition.
approved_indications: Lumbar axial and radicular pain and diabetic neuropathy pain, for which the cited RCTs suggest superior efficacy
therapies_index.administration: 10 kHz.

therapies_index.name: Burst SCS
therapies_index.mechanism: Low-amplitude, paresthesia-free bursts influence medial and lateral sensory pathways.

therapies_index.name: Closed-loop tonic SCS
therapies_index.mechanism: Evoked-potential feedback regulates the amplitude of tonic stimulation.

therapies_index.name: DRG stimulation
approved_indications: Focal neuropathic pain, particularly CRPS and PSPS
Localized neurogenic pain, including groin pain
therapies_index.administration: Lead placement above T10, to a maximum of C6, is advised only for clinicians with recognized DRG stimulation expertise.
key_toxicities: Vascular and neurologic injury, with greater risk for cervical and thoracic placement

therapies_index.name: PNS
approved_indications: Localized neurogenic pain when SCS poses substantial risks; supporting evidence is limited

therapies_index.name: peripheral nerve field stimulation
approved_indications: Localized neurogenic pain, with limited evidence for PNS

therapies_index.name: occipital nerve stimulation
approved_indications: Chronic migraine, which accounts for most of the cited PNS evidence

therapies_index.name: sacral nerve root stimulation
approved_indications: Pelvic and bladder pain or bladder dysfunction; evidence for interstitial cystitis and bladder pain syndrome is limited

therapies_index.name: L2MB NMES
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides restorative neuromuscular electrical stimulation at the L2 medial branch.
approved_indications: Chronic axial mechanical low back pain, supported by moderate evidence

therapies_index.name: paddle leads
approved_indications: SCS cases needing greater lead stability or in which percutaneous access is unsuitable
therapies_index.administration: Placement requires a trained neurosurgeon, preoperative MRI planning, and secure anchoring.

therapies_index.name: percutaneous leads
key_toxicities: Compared with paddle leads, the guide describes a greater migration risk.

therapies_index.name: epidural blood patch
approved_indications: Cerebrospinal fluid leak or spinal headache after dural breach when conservative care does not resolve the condition

therapies_index.name: surgical decompression
approved_indications: Epidural hematoma after an SCS procedure
therapies_index.administration: Undertake promptly, ideally within 24 hours of symptom onset.

therapies_index.name: device removal
approved_indications: Deep infection involving an SCS device
Superficial infection that does not respond to treatment
therapies_index.administration: For deep infection, combine with surgical debridement and extended culture-guided antibiotics. Defer reimplantation for a minimum of 12 weeks after removal for infection and place the new device on the contralateral side.
monitoring: Confirm that infection has fully resolved before reimplantation.

therapies_index.name: surgical debridement
approved_indications: Deep infection after SCS implantation
therapies_index.administration: Perform with device removal and extended culture-guided antibiotic treatment.

therapies_index.name: cefazolin
approved_indications: First-line antibiotic prophylaxis against surgical infection during SCS procedures
therapies_index.administration: Give within 30–60 min before incision; the guide also specifies administration within 60 minutes before skin incision. Redose for procedures lasting >2 h or with significant blood loss, and avoid continuation beyond 24 h postoperatively.

therapies_index.name: clindamycin
approved_indications: An alternative for surgical infection prevention in cases of resistance, selected according to local resistance patterns and infectious disease specialist guidance

therapies_index.name: vancomycin
approved_indications: An alternative for surgical infection prevention in cases of resistance, selected according to local resistance patterns and infectious disease specialist guidance
therapies_index.administration: When used as sole prophylaxis, administer 120 minutes before skin incision.

therapies_index.name: teicoplanin
approved_indications: An alternative for surgical infection prevention in cases of resistance, selected according to local resistance patterns and infectious disease specialist guidance

therapies_index.name: mupirocin
approved_indications: Preprocedural nasal decolonization in patients carrying S aureus
therapies_index.administration: Apply nasal mupirocin 2% ointment for 5 d preprocedure, together with daily chlorhexidine gluconate body washes.
monitoring: Seek infectious disease specialist guidance for mupirocin resistance or allergy.

therapies_index.name: chlorhexidine gluconate
approved_indications: Preprocedural body washing for patients carrying S aureus
therapies_index.administration: Use for daily body washes for 5 d preprocedure alongside nasal mupirocin 2% ointment.
monitoring: Seek infectious disease specialist guidance if the patient has a chlorhexidine allergy.

therapies_index.name: chlorhexidine
approved_indications: Antiseptic skin preparation before an SCS procedure
therapies_index.administration: Allow adequate drying after skin application. The guide says chlorhexidine or alcohol-containing solutions should not be used for antimicrobial wound irrigation.

therapies_index.name: povidone-iodine
approved_indications: Antiseptic skin preparation before an SCS procedure
therapies_index.administration: Allow adequate drying after application.

therapies_index.name: tapentadol
approved_indications: An atypical opioid to which rotation is advised before an SCS trial or implantation in the context of opioid rationalization
monitoring: Assess opioid use before an SCS trial or implantation.

therapies_index.name: buprenorphine
approved_indications: An atypical opioid to which rotation is advised before an SCS trial or implantation in the context of opioid rationalization
monitoring: Assess opioid use before an SCS trial or implantation.

therapies_index.name: warfarin
therapies_index.administration: Stop 5 d before surgery. Table 6 advises resuming anticoagulants 24 h postprocedure unless contraindicated; Table 9 specifies 24 h for low-risk cases and 48 h for high-risk cases.
key_toxicities: Anticoagulation increases bleeding risk during SCS procedures, including the risk of epidural hematoma.
monitoring: Confirm the international normalized ratio before the procedure.
Monitor for bleeding during and after the procedure.

therapies_index.name: clopidogrel
therapies_index.administration: Stop 7 d before an SCS procedure.

therapies_index.name: aspirin
therapies_index.administration: For primary prophylaxis, stop 6 d before the procedure. For secondary prophylaxis, weigh cardiovascular and procedural risks through shared decision-making.
monitoring: Assess cardiovascular and procedural risks when it is used for secondary prophylaxis.

therapies_index.name: topical anesthetics
approved_indications: Persistent IPG pocket pain
therapies_index.administration: Apply topically; the guide does not specify a dose or schedule.

therapies_index.name: cognitive behavioral therapy
approved_indications: Pain catastrophizing identified during psychological preparation for SCS, to improve readiness and adherence

therapies_index.name: physical therapy
approved_indications: Preprocedural physical conditioning and support for opioid tapering
Postimplantation rehabilitation focused on safe mobilization and motor control
therapies_index.administration: The guide recommends incorporating it into multimodal rehabilitation after implantation; it does not give a session schedule.
monitoring: Assess functional improvement and counsel on a gradual return to activity while limiting the risk of lead migration or hardware complications.

recognition: Injury may result from direct trauma, compression associated with bleeding, or impaired blood supply.
Complex anatomy, obesity, and repeat procedures increase risk.
prevention: Plan the procedure carefully and monitor closely afterward.
Use shallow needle angles and oblique fluoroscopic views.
Arrange prompt assessment and access to emergency imaging and neurosurgical or spinal services if neurologic symptoms occur.

toxicities.event: Vascular or neurologic injury during DRG stimulation
toxicities.incidence: Neurologic complication rates with DRG stimulation range from 0%–8.8%.
recognition: Vascular injury is more likely with DRG stimulation than with midline SCS because of potential mechanical impingement.
Cervical and thoracic placements carry greater vascular and neurologic risk.
prevention: Select patients and plan lead placement carefully.

Restrict placement above T10, up to a maximum of C6, to clinicians with recognized DRG stimulation expertise; obtain multidisciplinary input, comprehensive informed consent, and documentation of the rationale and risk–benefit assessment.

recognition: Minor bleeding is common; more substantial bleeding may cause an epidural or generator-pocket hematoma.
Anticoagulants and supplements that affect coagulation increase bleeding risk.
Observe for hematoma formation during and after the procedure.

management.actions: Obtain urgent MRI to establish its extent and guide treatment. Perform timely surgical decompression, ideally within 24 hours of symptom onset, to reduce the risk of permanent neurologic damage.

prevention: Assess coagulation and anticoagulant or antiplatelet use individually.
Maintain hemostasis during implantation and monitor for bleeding afterward.

toxicities.event: Dural breach, cerebrospinal fluid leak, and spinal headache
toxicities.incidence: Dural breach occurs in 0.2%–2% of cases.
recognition: A dural breach can produce a cerebrospinal fluid leak and spinal headache.
Spinal stenosis, adhesions, and obesity are associated with these breaches.

management.actions: An epidural blood patch may be required.

prevention: Plan the procedure carefully and check for symptoms during trial follow-up.

recognition: The risk is of particular concern in patients with severe comorbidities.
prevention: Plan anesthesia carefully before surgery.
Keep sedation as light as feasible while maintaining comfort and limiting excessive movement; consider deeper sedation or full anesthesia according to patient and procedural factors.

toxicities.incidence: Overall infection rates are 2% to 4%; deep infections occur in 1% to 2.5% of cases.
recognition: Infection usually becomes apparent ≥3 d after surgery, with inflammation, disproportionate pain, purulent drainage, or fever.
Inflammatory markers can be elevated but may remain normal.
Diabetes, immunosuppression, smoking, prolonged trials, high opioid doses, and S aureus colonization are risk factors; preoperative hospitalization increases risk fourfold.
Examination alone may not reliably distinguish superficial from deep infection.

management.actions: Use blood tests and imaging, such as computed tomography or MRI, to establish whether deep infection or an epidural abscess is present.
Wait a minimum of 12 weeks before reimplantation to allow complete infection resolution, and place the replacement device on the contralateral side.

prevention: Screen patients undergoing SCS trials or implantation for S aureus carriage and decolonize carriers.
Apply perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis and strict surgical infection-control practices.
Avoid unnecessarily prolonged trials, inspect wounds, and educate patients about infection symptoms.

recognition: Usually appears in the first 7–14 d after implantation.
Limited to skin and subcutaneous tissue, with incision-site erythema, pain, swelling, or drainage.

management.actions: Give oral antibiotics for 7–10 d. Device removal is generally unnecessary unless the infection fails to respond.

prevention: Follow the recommended perioperative infection-prevention measures and monitor the wound.

toxicities.incidence: Deep infections occur in 1% to 2.5% of cases.
recognition: Can develop within 90 d after implantation.
May involve deep soft tissue, muscle, fascia, and the device; wound separation, purulent drainage, or device erosion may occur.
Possible complications include epidural abscess, osteomyelitis, and meningitis.

management.actions: Remove the device, surgically debride the affected area, and provide extended antibiotics guided by cultures. Infectious disease specialist involvement is recommended.

prevention: Use the recommended screening, decolonization, antibiotic prophylaxis, aseptic technique, and wound surveillance measures.

toxicities.incidence: Persistent IPG pocket pain occurs in 5%–20% of cases.
recognition: Persistent pain at the generator pocket may be related to battery size or placement.
prevention: Choose the IPG with regard to the patient's anatomy and preferences, and create a suitable pocket with minimal tissue disruption.

recognition: A seroma or hygroma may form at the device pocket.

management.actions: Treatment may include aspiration and placement of a binder.

prevention: Minimize tissue disruption and eliminate dead space when creating and closing the pocket.

toxicities.incidence: With SCS, lead migration occurs in 2%–10% of cases.
recognition: Migration, usually associated with inadequate anchoring, reduces stimulation efficacy but does not itself pose a neurologic threat.

management.actions: Repositioning the lead may restore function.

prevention: Secure leads with mechanical or suture anchors.
Counsel patients about postoperative activity restrictions and gradual return to activity.
Monitor for migration during trials and after implantation.

toxicities.event: Device malfunction, battery failure, allergic reaction, or lead adhesion
recognition: Hardware malfunction or battery failure can affect device operation.
Allergic reactions are rare.
Lead adhesions may diminish stimulation delivery over time.

management.actions: Assess device performance at regular follow-up and address complications promptly.

prevention: Provide instruction on device operation and arrange ongoing device monitoring.

recognition: Stimulation may become less effective because of tolerance or changes in pain perception.

management.actions: Arrange regular review and reprogram the device as needed.

prevention: Maintain follow-up, educate patients and caregivers, and adjust the device when necessary.

recognition: Hypersensitivity to stimulation without paresthesia may allow relative overstimulation to provoke pain over time.

management.actions: Consider a graduated approach to amplitude and intermittent dosing.

prevention: Use graduated amplitude adjustments and intermittent dosing as mitigation strategies.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use a first-generation cephalosporin such as cefazolin before SCS incision. Give antibiotics within 30–60 min before incision; the guideline also specifies within 60 minutes before skin incision, or 120 minutes beforehand when vancomycin is used for mono-prophylaxis. Consult a local infectious disease specialist for β-lactam allergy. Where resistance warrants an alternative, clindamycin, vancomycin, or teicoplanin may be selected according to local resistance patterns with specialist advice. Redose for a procedure lasting >2 h or substantial blood loss, use weight-based dosing, and avoid prophylactic antibiotics beyond 24 h postoperatively.
prophylaxis.duration: Within 30–60 min before incision; 120 minutes before incision for vancomycin mono-prophylaxis; not beyond 24 h postoperatively

prophylaxis.recommendation: Screen for nasal S aureus carriage, including methicillin-resistant strains. For carriers, use nasal mupirocin 2% ointment and daily chlorhexidine gluconate body washes for 5 d before the procedure. Seek infectious disease advice for MRSA colonization, mupirocin resistance, or allergy to mupirocin or chlorhexidine.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing an SCS trial or implantation; decolonization applies to those with positive screening

prophylaxis.recommendation: Treat infections elsewhere, optimize blood glucose, and discontinue tobacco use. Perform a surgical scrub for 2–5 min, avoid artificial nails, and use clippers if hair removal is needed.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients and surgical personnel involved in SCS implantation

prophylaxis.recommendation: Maintain sterile equipment, hand hygiene, aseptic practice, and frequent glove changes. Wear a mask, cap, sterile gown, and gloves; double gloving is recommended. Prepare skin with chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine and allow adequate drying; consider iodophor-impregnated drapes for high-risk cases. Limit operating-room traffic, maintain hemostasis, avoid dead space, minimize operative time, and use laminar flow with high-efficiency particulate air filtration.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing SCS implantation and their surgical teams

prophylaxis.type: Wound closure and postoperative infection prevention
prophylaxis.recommendation: Irrigate with saline before closing the wound, approximate its edges, eliminate dead space, and minimize tension. Antimicrobial irrigation may be considered for patients at high risk, but chlorhexidine- or alcohol-containing solutions should not be used for this purpose. Apply an occlusive dressing and teach wound care, hand hygiene during dressing changes, and recognition of surgical-site infection. The use of antiseptic wound dressings remains controversial.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing SCS implantation; antimicrobial irrigation is considered for those at high risk

prophylaxis.recommendation: Assess anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, and coagulopathy individually. Stop warfarin 5 d before surgery and confirm the international normalized ratio before the procedure; stop clopidogrel 7 d beforehand. Allow 5 half-lives after stopping newer anticoagulants. Use bridging only for patients at high risk of clotting and with advice from their hematologist, cardiologist, or neurologist. Stop supplements affecting coagulation, such as fish oil, garlic, and gingko biloba. For altered coagulation, obtain preoperative neuraxial MRI or computed tomography to reduce epidural hematoma risk.
prophylaxis.target_population: SCS candidates taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents, or with coagulopathy
prophylaxis.duration: Warfarin: 5 d before surgery; clopidogrel: 7 d before; newer anticoagulants: 5 half-lives before the procedure

prophylaxis.recommendation: Stop aspirin used for primary prophylaxis before SCS. When aspirin is used for secondary prophylaxis, weigh cardiovascular and procedural risks through shared decision-making. Stop nonaspirin nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs before SCS.
prophylaxis.target_population: SCS candidates taking aspirin or nonaspirin nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs
prophylaxis.duration: Aspirin for primary prophylaxis: 6 d before the procedure; nonaspirin nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs: 5 half-lives before SCS

prophylaxis.recommendation: Monitor for bleeding during and after SCS. Resume anticoagulants unless contraindicated, with timing based on bleeding risk.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients requiring anticoagulants after an SCS procedure
prophylaxis.duration: 24 h postprocedure for low-risk cases; 48 h for high-risk cases

prophylaxis.type: Prevention of procedural injury and lead migration
prophylaxis.recommendation: Plan lead placement with MRI assessment of epidural anatomy and use fluoroscopy for accurate positioning. Position patients to permit epidural access and prevent pressure injuries, use meticulous tissue handling, and secure leads with mechanical or suture anchors. For cervical lead placement, intraoperative neuromonitoring is recommended when difficulty is anticipated but is not routinely needed for T12 entry.

Maintain direct communication and daily follow-up during an SCS trial. Inspect wounds for infection, hematoma, and poor healing; monitor for neurologic symptoms, lead migration, and device problems. Ensure urgent review, emergency imaging, and referral pathways for time-critical complications. Educate patients about when to seek medical attention.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing an SCS trial or permanent implantation
prophylaxis.duration: Daily during the trial; initial wound follow-up within 1–2 wk, with further assessments as needed

infection_management.prevention: Screen patients before an SCS trial or implantation. Treat carriers with nasal mupirocin 2% ointment and daily chlorhexidine gluconate body washes for 5 d preprocedure.
infection_management.management: Seek infectious disease specialist guidance for MRSA colonization, mupirocin resistance, or allergy to mupirocin or chlorhexidine.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: SCS-related infection associated with S aureus or S epidermidis
infection_management.prevention: These are the principal pathogens identified for SCS-related infection. Use perioperative infection-control measures and antibiotic prophylaxis; cefazolin is first-line for surgical infection prevention.
infection_management.management: For suspected surgical-site infection, select antibiotics according to local resistance and culture results. When resistance requires an alternative for prophylaxis, clindamycin, vancomycin, or teicoplanin may be considered with infectious disease specialist guidance.

infection_management.prevention: Apply the recommended infection-prevention practices, inspect the wound, and explain infection signs to patients.
infection_management.management: Treat with oral antibiotics for 7–10 d. Device removal is usually unnecessary unless treatment fails.

infection_management.prevention: Use screening and decolonization, timely antibiotic prophylaxis, strict asepsis, and postoperative wound surveillance.
infection_management.management: Use blood tests and computed tomography or MRI to assess suspected deep infection and complications. Remove the device, surgically debride infected tissue, and give extended culture-guided antibiotics; infectious disease specialist involvement is recommended. If removal is necessary, defer reimplantation for a minimum of 12 weeks until infection has fully resolved and implant the new device on the contralateral side.

infection_management.prevention: Apply the recommended perioperative infection-prevention measures and recognize possible deep infection promptly.
infection_management.management: These complications of deep infection require urgent intervention; imaging can help detect an epidural abscess.

infection_management.prevention: Apply the recommended measures to prevent SCS-related infection.
infection_management.management: The guideline identifies osteomyelitis as a possible complication of deep infection but does not specify separate treatment beyond the management described for deep infection.

conditions.name: chronic, refractory pain
conditions.description: Persistent pain that has not responded adequately to standard medical treatment; SCS is considered after comprehensive multidisciplinary management.

subtypes.name: Neuropathic pain
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guideline identifies refractory neuropathic pain as a principal indication for SCS.

subtypes.name: Mixed pain
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Includes pain with both neuropathic and nociceptive components, such as some postsurgical pain.

subtypes.name: Nociplastic pain
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Includes widespread pain syndromes and fibromyalgia; evidence for SCS is limited.

subtypes.name: Nociceptive pain and neuromuscular dysfunction
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Includes mechanical and nociceptive axial low back pain, for which SCS has minimal efficacy; the guideline describes moderate evidence for restorative neuromuscular electrical stimulation (L2 medial branch).

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess epidural anatomy and plan lead placement; identify central canal stenosis that would prevent safe epidural lead insertion.
Identify active or insufficiently managed disorders and factors such as pain catastrophizing that may impair outcomes or engagement.
Identify colonization, including methicillin-resistant S aureus, before an SCS trial or implantation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before an SCS trial or implantation
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A positive result calls for a carrier decolonization protocol.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Check coagulation status before the procedure in patients who have stopped warfarin.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before SCS surgery in patients taking warfarin

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess neuraxial anatomy and reduce epidural hematoma risk.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before the procedure in patients with altered coagulation

diagnostic_workup.test: numeric rating scale or visual analog scale
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure pain reduction during the SCS trial alongside functional improvement.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Trial success is defined by >50% pain reduction together with improved function.

prognostic_tools.name: SCS trial
components: Pain reduction on the numeric rating scale or visual analog scale
Patient-reported quality of life and activities of daily living

risk_groups.criteria: >50% pain reduction on the numeric rating scale or visual analog scale and improved function
risk_groups.expected_outcome: The guideline identifies trial success as an important predictor of longer-term benefit from permanent implantation.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Mobility, endurance, and other relevant functional tasks should also be evaluated independently. Lower baseline opioid use and favorable psychosocial factors are additional predictors of longer-term success.

follow_up.schedule: Maintain daily contact during the SCS trial. An initial wound review is recommended within 1–2 wk; programming reviews are suggested at 2–4 wk, 3 mo, 6 mo, and 12 mo, with additional visits when needed. Assess treatment effectiveness at 6 mo and annually.
recommended_tests: Inspect the wound for infection, hematoma, and impaired healing.
Assess pain, medication use, function, quality of life, and device performance.
Evaluate suspected deep device infection with blood tests and computed tomography or MRI.
long_term_effects: Stimulation may become less effective over time.
Pain perception may change over time.
Lead migration, hardware malfunction, and infection can affect sustained benefit.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Ongoing device adjustment, patient education, and access to urgent review are important after implantation.

conditions.name: PSPS
conditions.description: A spinal pain condition encompassing presentations both without prior surgery and after surgery. The guideline cites RCTs and long-term observational studies supporting SCS for this indication.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guideline identifies personalized physical and psychosocial rehabilitation as a potential means of improving return to work; reported return-to-work rates after SCS are 9.5% to 14% across patients.

conditions.name: PSPS type 1
conditions.description: The PSPS subtype in which spinal surgery has not been performed.

conditions.name: PSPS type 2
conditions.description: The PSPS subtype arising after spinal surgery.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guideline notes that the OPERA RCT is expected to inform post-SCS rehabilitation protocols, particularly for this subtype.

conditions.name: CRPS
conditions.description: SCS is described as effective for localized CRPS, but less effective when CRPS is widespread or predominantly nociceptive. DRG stimulation is discussed for focal neuropathic pain, particularly CRPS.

subtypes.name: localized CRPS
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Localized presentation for which the guideline reports better SCS effectiveness.

subtypes.name: widespread or nociceptive-predominant CRPS
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Presentation for which the guideline reports lower SCS effectiveness.

subtypes.name: upper extremity complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed among carefully selected indications for cervical SCS.

subtypes.name: lower extremity CRPS
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guideline describes DRG stimulation as effective for this presentation.

conditions.name: PDN
conditions.description: The guideline presents SCS as an emerging option and states that recent RCTs found moderate efficacy for pain reduction.

conditions.name: Peripheral vascular disease
conditions.description: The guideline discusses SCS for pain and ischemic symptoms in critical limb ischemia, while noting that the evidence is chiefly observational.

subtypes.name: critical limb ischemia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The ischemic condition specifically identified as a possible SCS indication.

conditions.name: critical limb ischemia
conditions.description: SCS may improve pain and ischemic symptoms; the supporting evidence described in the guideline is primarily observational.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Pain and ischemic symptoms are the treatment targets identified.

conditions.name: Refractory angina
conditions.description: The guideline describes SCS use in selected patients when other treatments have failed and notes a lack of high-quality RCTs.

conditions.name: Nociplastic pain
conditions.description: A pain phenotype for which the guideline describes limited evidence for SCS and emphasizes careful patient selection.

subtypes.name: Widespread pain syndromes
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed as an example of this phenotype.

subtypes.name: fibromyalgia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed as an example of this phenotype.

conditions.name: Mechanical and nociceptive axial low back pain
synonyms: chronic axial mechanical low back pain
conditions.description: The guideline reports minimal SCS efficacy for this pain pattern, with better SCS results in mixed pain, and cites moderate evidence for restorative neuromuscular electrical stimulation (L2 medial branch).

conditions.name: Postsurgical pain with neuropathic and nociceptive pain
conditions.description: A mixed-pain presentation for which the guideline reports moderate evidence of SCS benefit.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Pain after surgery with both neuropathic and nociceptive components.

conditions.name: pelvic and visceral pain
conditions.description: The guideline groups these among emerging SCS indications that require careful selection and auditing; it describes limited evidence for visceral pain.

subtypes.name: interstitial cystitis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Named as an example of an emerging indication; evidence for sacral nerve root stimulation is limited.

subtypes.name: chronic pancreatitis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Named among the visceral pain conditions studied with T4–T8 SCS.

subtypes.name: gastroparesis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Named among the conditions studied with T4–T8 SCS.

conditions.name: interstitial cystitis
conditions.description: Listed as an emerging pelvic or visceral pain indication requiring careful selection and auditing; the guideline reports limited evidence for sacral nerve root stimulation.

conditions.name: cervical radicular pain
conditions.description: Identified as a condition for which the guideline supports cervical SCS in carefully selected cases, citing evidence of moderate benefit.

conditions.name: cervical axial pain
conditions.description: Identified as a condition for which the guideline supports cervical SCS in carefully selected cases, citing evidence of moderate benefit.

conditions.name: persistent spinal pain syndrome (cervical)
conditions.description: A cervical pain presentation for which the guideline supports cervical SCS in carefully selected cases, citing evidence of moderate benefit.

conditions.name: chronic migraine
conditions.description: Listed among conditions studied with cervical SCS and peripheral nerve stimulation; the guideline describes limited evidence for stimulation in cephalgia and identifies occipital nerve stimulation as the best-supported peripheral nerve stimulation application.

conditions.name: occipital neuralgia
conditions.description: Listed among conditions studied with C2–C3 SCS; the guideline describes limited evidence for stimulation in cephalgia.

conditions.name: cervicogenic headache
conditions.description: Listed among conditions studied with C2–C3 SCS; the guideline describes limited evidence for stimulation in cephalgia.

conditions.name: Localized neurogenic pain

subtypes.name: groin pain

subtypes.name: lower extremity postamputation pain
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed among presentations studied with PNS/peripheral nerve field stimulation/ NMES.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients being considered for neurostimulation after standard medical therapies have provided insufficient relief.
decision_rules: Use multimodal conservative management within a multidisciplinary framework before considering neurostimulation; tailor its duration to the condition and the patient's response.
Consider neurostimulation without unnecessary delay when pain remains refractory, particularly in PSPS or CRPS.

recommended_regimens.name: conservative management
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide a multimodal course of conservative treatment before deciding on neurostimulation.

response_assessment.method: Assess pain relief, functional improvement and response to standard therapies.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistently refractory pain supports consideration of timely neurostimulation.

supportive_care: Coordinate assessment and treatment through a multidisciplinary team.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Extending conservative treatment without meaningful improvement may postpone an effective intervention.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Appropriately selected patients whose refractory pain or function has not improved adequately despite comprehensive multidisciplinary management.
decision_rules: Consider the pain phenotype, anatomical distribution, psychosocial factors and ability to participate in treatment before selecting stimulation.
Do not proceed when an absolute contraindication makes implantation unsafe; assess modifiable relative contraindications individually.

recommended_regimens.name: SCS
recommended_regimens.summary: Use spinal cord stimulation for appropriately selected refractory neuropathic pain.

alternative_regimens.name: DRG stimulation

alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider particularly for localized pain, including CRPS or PSPS.

alternative_regimens.name: PNS

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: SCS targets may be selected along the accessible cord from C2 to the conus according to the pain mechanism and anatomy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Appropriately selected patients with refractory postsurgical pain containing neuropathic and nociceptive components.
decision_rules: Consider SCS when comprehensive multidisciplinary care has not produced sufficient pain relief or functional improvement.
Individualize the stimulation target to the pain distribution and underlying mechanisms.

recommended_regimens.name: SCS
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat selected refractory pain with mixed mechanisms, including postsurgical neuropathic and nociceptive pain.

supportive_care: Continue multidisciplinary assessment and rehabilitation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline describes T8–T11 SCS as effective for mixed neuropathic and nociplastic pain mechanisms.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with refractory PSPS type 1 (no surgery performed) or type 2 (postsurgery) after multidisciplinary conservative management.
decision_rules: Consider neurostimulation in a timely manner if conservative treatment has not produced meaningful improvement.
Select lead targets according to the anatomical distribution; the guideline lists T8–T11 SCS for lumbar, leg and lower-body presentations.
Consider DRG stimulation when the neuropathic pain is focal.

recommended_regimens.name: SCS
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat eligible refractory PSPS type 1 or type 2; supporting evidence includes RCTs and long-term observational studies.

alternative_regimens.name: DRG stimulation
alternative_regimens.summary: Provide targeted neuromodulation for focal neuropathic pain in PSPS.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when the patient's pain distribution favors focal stimulation.

supportive_care: Assess psychosocial readiness and optimize participation in rehabilitation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: PSPS was previously called failed back surgery syndrome.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with refractory, particularly localized CRPS; benefit from SCS is less favorable when pain is widespread or predominantly nociceptive.
decision_rules: Consider timely neurostimulation after inadequate response to multidisciplinary conservative care.
Use the site and extent of pain to choose between cord and focal DRG targets.

recommended_regimens.name: DRG stimulation

supportive_care: Use multidisciplinary input for patient selection and procedural planning.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Appropriately selected patients with refractory painful diabetic neuropathy.
decision_rules: Consider SCS after insufficient benefit from standard therapies and multidisciplinary management.
Individualize stimulation mode to the patient's phenotype and anatomy.

recommended_regimens.name: SCS
recommended_regimens.summary: An emerging treatment option for refractory PDN; recent RCTs indicate moderate efficacy for reducing pain.

alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Select the stimulation mode according to individual response, pain phenotype and anatomy.

supportive_care: Optimize blood glucose before implantation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The evidence for selecting newer stimulation modes is still developing.

alternative_regimens.name: SCS
alternative_regimens.summary: May alleviate pain and ischemic symptoms in critical limb ischemia.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Use individualized, multidisciplinary assessment and informed consent when other viable approaches are lacking.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence for ischemic pain indications is principally observational.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected patients whose angina persists despite other treatments.
decision_rules: Consider SCS only in selected cases after other treatments have failed.

alternative_regimens.name: SCS
alternative_regimens.summary: An option for selected refractory angina, subject to the limitations of the available evidence.

Where robust evidence is absent, base any treatment consideration on expert opinion, multidisciplinary input, clinical need, lack of viable alternatives and comprehensive informed consent; document the risk–benefit rationale.

alternative_regimens.name: SCS

alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Use only after individualized assessment of the evidence, alternatives and risks.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline does not present SCS as an established treatment for widespread pain syndromes or fibromyalgia.

Consider the distinct evidence for restorative stimulation of the L2 medial branch.

alternative_regimens.name: L2MB NMES
alternative_regimens.summary: Restorative neuromuscular electrical stimulation for chronic axial mechanical low back pain.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider in the chronic axial mechanical low back pain phenotype.

supportive_care: Address physical conditioning and consider physical therapy.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline reports minimal efficacy for SCS in this predominantly nociceptive phenotype, rather than explicitly prohibiting its use.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Carefully selected patients with emerging indications, including interstitial cystitis or other pelvic and visceral pain.
decision_rules: When evidence is limited, consider stimulation using multidisciplinary input, assessment of clinical need and alternatives, informed consent, and documentation of risks and benefits.
Audit outcomes in patients treated for emerging indications.

Choose a target according to pain location: the guideline lists T4–T8 SCS for visceral pain, T8–T11 or T10–T12 SCS for some pelvic distributions, and sacral nerve root stimulation for pelvic or bladder presentations.

alternative_regimens.name: SCS
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered for selected pelvic or visceral pain indications.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Requires careful patient selection and auditing.

alternative_regimens.name: Sacral nerve root stimulation
alternative_regimens.summary: A target described for pelvic and bladder pain or bladder dysfunction.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider the limited evidence for interstitial cystitis and bladder pain syndrome.

supportive_care: Use comprehensive informed consent and multidisciplinary review.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline characterizes pelvic and visceral pain as emerging indications rather than established indications supported by robust evidence.
