Place leads between C2 and C6 where appropriate; the guideline supports epidural entry at C7–T4 or T11–L1 for navigation to cervical targets.

recommended_regimens.name: cervical SCS
recommended_regimens.summary: A supported option in carefully selected cervical radicular pain, on evidence indicating moderate benefit.

supportive_care: Use imaging guidance and precise surgical technique.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Cervical procedures require accredited training, supervised practice and attention to anatomical risk.

treatment_pathways.condition: upper extremity complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)
treatment_pathways.patient_population: Carefully selected patients with upper extremity CRPS.
decision_rules: Select cervical stimulation targets according to the patient's distribution and imaging findings.
Consider the guideline's limited evidence for C7–T4 SCS in shoulder-arm and scapula/upper dorsal regional pain.

recommended_regimens.name: cervical SCS
recommended_regimens.summary: A supported treatment in selected upper extremity CRPS, on evidence indicating moderate benefit.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Cervical lead placement calls for specialist procedural competence and individualized consideration of risk.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Carefully selected patients with cervical axial pain.
decision_rules: Consider cervical SCS according to anatomy and pain phenotype while acknowledging the limited evidence specifically described for neck pain.

recommended_regimens.name: cervical SCS
recommended_regimens.summary: A supported option for selected cervical axial pain within the guideline's cervical neurostimulation recommendations.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The cervical neurostimulation discussion refers to moderate benefit, while the target-region table characterizes evidence for neck pain as limited.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Carefully selected patients with cervical persistent spinal pain syndrome.
decision_rules: Choose cervical lead positioning with imaging and precise technique according to the pain distribution.

recommended_regimens.name: cervical SCS
recommended_regimens.summary: A supported option for selected cervical persistent spinal pain syndrome, on evidence indicating moderate benefit.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline identifies C2 to C6 as the optimal range for cervical lead placement.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with focal neuropathic pain, including groin pain or localized CRPS.
decision_rules: Consider DRG stimulation when pain is focal.
For DRG lead placement above T10, up to a maximum of the C6 level, restrict the procedure to clinicians with recognized DRG expertise.

recommended_regimens.name: DRG stimulation
recommended_regimens.summary: An advanced neuromodulation treatment recommended for focal neuropathic pain.

alternative_regimens.name: PNS
alternative_regimens.summary: Targets localized neurogenic pain outside the cord.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: May be useful when SCS entails significant risk.

supportive_care: Obtain comprehensive informed consent and document the clinical rationale and risk–benefit assessment.
Use multidisciplinary input for higher DRG placements.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: DRG implantation entails risks including IPG-site pain, lead migration, fracture and infection; cervical and thoracic placements have greater vascular and neurologic injury risk. Some evidence suggests better efficacy than traditional SCS for focal neuropathic pain, with sustained long-term benefit.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected patients with chronic migraine.
decision_rules: Treat stimulation for this cephalic pain indication as a limited-evidence consideration requiring careful selection.

alternative_regimens.name: PNS
alternative_regimens.summary: The guideline identifies occipital nerve stimulation as the best-supported PNS application for chronic migraine.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider only after individualized evaluation of limited evidence and treatment alternatives.

alternative_regimens.name: C2–C7 SCS
alternative_regimens.summary: A studied cervical cord target for chronic migraine and other cephalic pain conditions.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The target-region discussion also identifies C2–C3 for occipital neuralgia and cervicogenic headache.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients selected for an SCS trial before possible permanent implantation.
decision_rules: Follow a trial-first approach in general.
Individualize trial length while recognizing that trials >ten days increase complications, particularly infections, without additional predictive value.
Use trial pain relief together with functional change and patient-reported outcomes to inform the permanent-implant decision.

recommended_regimens.name: SCS trial
recommended_regimens.summary: Test clinical response during everyday activities before deciding whether to implant permanently.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Trial success is defined by >50% pain reduction on the numeric rating scale or visual analog scale together with improved function.

alternative_regimens.name: direct SCS implantation
alternative_regimens.summary: Implantation without a preceding trial may be considered in suitable patients. The UK-based TRIAL-STIM study found no significant difference in long-term outcomes between trial-first and direct implantation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A multidisciplinary assessment strongly favors benefit, and the implanter has an implant-to-trial ratio >80% and has performed >100 implants.

response_assessment.timepoint: At completion of the SCS trial
response_assessment.method: Measure pain with the numeric rating scale or visual analog scale; independently assess mobility, endurance and relevant tasks, alongside quality of life and activities of daily living.
response_assessment.interpretation: >50% pain reduction with improved function indicates trial success and is a key predictor of longer-term benefit from permanent implantation.

supportive_care: Maintain daily contact and follow-up during the trial to detect complications, including dural puncture headache or lead migration.
Ensure urgent assessment is available for time-critical complications.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Lower baseline opioid use and favorable psychosocial factors also predict longer-term success; opioid doses <90 mg OMEDD are associated with better outcomes.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients taking opioids who are preparing for an SCS trial or implantation.
decision_rules: Rationalize opioid treatment before SCS and reduce use before a trial when feasible.
Consider rotation to tapentadol and/or buprenorphine before trial or implantation; where opioid intolerant, prefer <90 mg oral morphine equivalent daily dose (OMEDD).

recommended_regimens.name: opioid rationalization
recommended_regimens.summary: Reduce opioid exposure before stimulation where feasible to improve the likelihood of treatment success.

alternative_regimens.name: tapentadol and/or buprenorphine
alternative_regimens.summary: Rotation to these atypical opioids before SCS trial or implantation is advisable.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider while rationalizing an existing opioid regimen.

response_assessment.method: Review opioid exposure and psychosocial readiness.
response_assessment.interpretation: Higher opioid doses are associated with poorer SCS outcomes; <90 mg OMEDD is associated with better outcomes.

supportive_care: Use behavioral therapies, physical rehabilitation and nonopioid pharmacotherapy to facilitate tapering and limit withdrawal symptoms.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline identifies high opioid use (>90 mg morphine equivalent daily dose) as a relative contraindication associated with poorer outcomes and more explantations. It attributes improved pain control and lower failure rates after preimplantation opioid weaning to the study by Nissen et al.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected patients proceeding to SCS implantation, including those whose pain or anatomy makes percutaneous access unsuitable.
decision_rules: Choose lead configuration according to anatomy, access and the need for stability.
Use paddle leads when greater stability is needed or percutaneous access is unsuitable; placement requires a trained neurosurgeon.

recommended_regimens.name: SCS
recommended_regimens.summary: Implant leads using preoperative planning, precise positioning, secure anchoring, careful tissue handling and infection-control practices.

recommended_regimens.name: paddle leads
recommended_regimens.summary: Use when enhanced stability is required or percutaneous implantation is unsuitable; the guideline describes greater efficacy and less migration in appropriate cases.

alternative_regimens.name: percutaneous leads
alternative_regimens.summary: A lead approach associated with fewer complications and less need for revision than paddle leads.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when percutaneous access is suitable and the need for paddle-lead stability does not predominate.

supportive_care: Obtain preoperative MRI to plan lead placement.
Use fluoroscopic guidance for lead positioning and secure anchoring to reduce migration.
Provide perioperative infection prevention and anticoagulation management appropriate to procedural risk.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Paddle-lead implantation requires advanced surgical skill and meticulous anchoring.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients after an SCS trial or permanent implantation.
decision_rules: Monitor wound healing, device performance, clinical benefit and complications after stimulation.
Adjust device programming when necessary, and address declining benefit or changes in pain perception during longer-term follow-up.
Offer a multimodal rehabilitation approach focused on safe movement, motor control and cognitive-behavioral techniques.

recommended_regimens.name: SCS follow-up and programming
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide structured surgical and outpatient monitoring, patient education, and device adjustments.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Initial wound follow-up within 1–2 wk; programming follow-up suggested at 2–4 wk, 3 mo, 6 mo, and 12 mo.

recommended_regimens.name: physical therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Include safe mobilization, motor control and cognitive-behavioral techniques in multimodal rehabilitation after implantation.

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 1–2 wk after implantation and subsequently as needed
response_assessment.method: Inspect the surgical site for infection, hematoma and inadequate healing.
response_assessment.interpretation: Concerning findings require prompt clinical review.

response_assessment.method: Review pain relief, function, device performance, programming needs and complications.
response_assessment.interpretation: Adjust stimulation or investigate complications according to findings.

response_assessment.method: Assess pain, medication use, function and quality of life as standardized treatment outcomes.

supportive_care: Educate patients and caregivers about wound care, activity restrictions, device operation, warning signs and access to urgent help.
Encourage a gradual return to activity while limiting the risk of lead migration or other hardware problems.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: There is no formal expert consensus or high-quality evidence directly comparing structured physiotherapy with standard postoperative care. Remote programming may be used when stable Wi-Fi is available, at the clinician's discretion.

special_populations.considerations: Opioid use above >90 mg morphine equivalent daily dose is associated with poorer SCS outcomes and more frequent explantation. Lower opioid use before a trial is associated with better long-term results.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Reduce opioid use before an SCS trial when feasible. Before trial or implantation, rotation to tapentadol and/or buprenorphine is advised; for opioid-intolerant patients, <90 mg oral morphine equivalent daily dose (OMEDD) is preferred. Behavioral therapies, physical rehabilitation, and nonopioid pharmacotherapy are recommended to support tapering.

special_populations.population: Patients receiving anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents, or with coagulopathy
special_populations.considerations: Bleeding risk requires an individual assessment before SCS, particularly because epidural hematoma can cause serious neurologic harm.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Stop warfarin 5 d before surgery and confirm the international normalized ratio before the procedure; stop clopidogrel 7 d beforehand. Allow 5 half-lives after newer anticoagulants and nonaspirin nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs. Stop aspirin used for primary prophylaxis 6 d beforehand; for secondary prophylaxis, weigh cardiovascular and procedural risks through shared decision-making. Reserve bridging therapy for patients at high risk of clotting, with specialist advice. Resume anticoagulants 24 h after the procedure in low-risk cases and 48 h after the procedure in high-risk cases.

special_populations.population: Patients with psychiatric disorders, cognitive impairment, or limited engagement
special_populations.considerations: Untreated major psychiatric disorders and substance use disorders are listed as absolute contraindications to SCS. Significant cognitive impairment may prevent effective device use or active participation in care. Severe depression, unrealistic expectations, poor coping, and unresolved social problems require evaluation before proceeding.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Address active or inadequately managed psychiatric conditions before implantation. Assess pain catastrophizing and recommend interventions such as cognitive behavioral therapy when indicated. Patients unable to participate actively in their care should not undergo implantation.

special_populations.population: Patients with excess weight, smoking, or poor physical conditioning
special_populations.considerations: These factors can worsen neurostimulation outcomes and increase the risks of infection, lead migration, or impaired wound healing. Severe obesity also increases procedural complexity and the risk of device failure.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Smoking cessation, weight loss, and physical therapy are recommended before treatment to improve surgical and functional outcomes.

special_populations.considerations: S aureus colonization increases the risk of infection associated with SCS. Patients undergoing a trial or implantation should be screened.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For positive screening results, prescribe nasal mupirocin 2% ointment and daily chlorhexidine gluconate body washes for 5 d before the procedure. Seek infectious disease specialist guidance for MRSA colonization, mupirocin resistance, or allergy to mupirocin or chlorhexidine.

special_populations.considerations: The usual first-generation cephalosporin prophylaxis requires individual consideration in this group.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consult a local infectious disease specialist about antibiotic prophylaxis.

special_populations.considerations: Cervical SCS is supported in carefully selected cases, including cervical radicular pain, upper extremity CRPS, cervical axial pain, and cervical PSPS, on the basis of evidence indicating moderate benefit.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Position leads between C2 and C6 using imaging and precise surgical technique. Supported epidural entry sites are C7–T4 or T11–L1, with anatomical factors considered. Practitioners must complete accredited training; proficiency in thoracic neuromodulation is advised before cervical cases.

special_populations.population: Patients requiring DRG lead placement above T10
special_populations.considerations: Cervical and thoracic DRG placement carries a higher risk of vascular and neurologic injury.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Placement above T10, up to a maximum of C6, should be performed only by clinicians with recognized DRG stimulation expertise, with multidisciplinary input, comprehensive informed consent, and documentation of the clinical rationale and risk-benefit assessment.

special_populations.population: Patients in rural or interstate areas
special_populations.considerations: Distance may limit access to postimplantation follow-up.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Telehealth and remote programming may improve access. Remote programming may be used when stable Wi-Fi is available, at the clinician’s discretion; referral networks can support shared care.

recommendations.statement: Offer SCS to appropriately selected patients with refractory neuropathic or mixed pain when comprehensive multidisciplinary care has not provided adequate pain relief or functional improvement.
Consider SCS for patients whose chronic, refractory pain has not responded to standard medical treatment, using defined selection criteria.
recommendations.rationale: Careful selection is important for treatment outcomes.

recommendations.statement: Do not use SCS when its risks exceed its potential benefits; assess modifiable risks individually with interdisciplinary input and shared decision-making.
Select the stimulation target individually according to the patient's pain mechanism and anatomy.
recommendations.rationale: Individualized targeting aims to improve benefit while limiting risk.
recommendations.source_heading: Targets for SCS and Peripheral Nerve Stimulation

recommendations.statement: Where support for a pain phenotype, indication, or stimulation target is limited, treatment may be considered using expert opinion, multidisciplinary input, clinical need, lack of viable alternatives, and comprehensive informed consent; document the risk–benefit reasoning.
recommendations.context: Indications or targets with limited evidence
recommendations.rationale: This approach supports transparent, patient-centered decisions.
recommendations.source_heading: Pain Phenotype, Indication, and Stimulation Target with Limited Evidence

recommendations.statement: Use cervical SCS in carefully selected patients with cervical radicular pain, upper extremity complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), cervical axial pain, or persistent spinal pain syndrome (cervical).
recommendations.rationale: The cited evidence indicates moderate benefit.

recommendations.statement: For cervical SCS, place leads optimally between C2 and C6 using imaging and precise surgical technique; epidural entry at C7–T4 or T11–L1 is supported, with anatomical factors taken into account.
recommendations.rationale: The entry sites permit navigation toward cervical targets.

recommendations.statement: Before performing cervical cases, complete accredited workshops and supervised training; proficiency in thoracic neuromodulation is advised. Maintain expertise with a minimum of ten SCS or dorsal root ganglion (DRG) procedures annually, alongside continuing education and peer review.
recommendations.rationale: Training and ongoing review support procedural safety.

recommendations.statement: Tailor the SCS stimulation mode to the patient's pain phenotype and anatomical factors.
recommendations.rationale: Responses differ, and evidence for newer modes is still developing.

recommendations.statement: Use DRG stimulation as an advanced option for focal neuropathic pain, particularly CRPS and persistent spinal pain syndrome (PSPS).
recommendations.rationale: Some evidence suggests greater efficacy than traditional SCS for focal neuropathic pain and sustained benefit.

recommendations.statement: Ensure clinicians undertaking DRG stimulation receive specialized training through accredited fellowships, practical workshops, and supervised practice.
recommendations.rationale: DRG procedures have specific device-related, vascular, and neurologic risks.

recommendations.statement: Restrict DRG lead placement above T10, up to a maximum of C6, to clinicians with recognized DRG stimulation expertise; obtain multidisciplinary input and comprehensive informed consent, and document the clinical reasoning and risk–benefit assessment.
recommendations.rationale: Cervical and thoracic placements carry greater vascular and neurologic injury risks.

recommendations.statement: Before considering neurostimulation, undertake multimodal conservative management within a multidisciplinary framework, typically for six to 12 months, adjusting the duration to the condition and response. Consider timely neurostimulation for refractory pain rather than prolonging ineffective conservative care.
recommendations.rationale: A conservative trial helps establish refractoriness, but unnecessary delay may postpone benefit, particularly in PSPS and CRPS.
recommendations.source_heading: Duration of Conservative Management Before Neurostimulation

recommendations.statement: Assess candidates' cognitive ability, realistic expectations, and motivation for rehabilitation; do not implant patients who cannot participate actively in their care, including those with significant cognitive impairment.
recommendations.rationale: Participation in follow-up, prescribed care, and psychosocial support is important to outcomes and complication management.

recommendations.statement: Rationalize opioid use for chronic noncancer pain before an SCS trial or implantation. Rotation to atypical opioids (tapentadol and/or buprenorphine) is advisable; if opioid intolerant, a dose of <90 mg oral morphine equivalent daily dose (OMEDD) is preferred. Reduce opioid use before trials when feasible.
recommendations.rationale: Higher opioid doses are associated with reduced SCS success; evidence supports weaning patients off opioids before implantation to reduce the risk of late device failure.

recommendations.statement: Use behavioral therapies, physical rehabilitation, and nonopioid pharmacotherapy together to support opioid tapering and prepare patients for SCS.
recommendations.rationale: A multimodal approach can help limit withdrawal symptoms.

recommendations.statement: Deliver neuromodulation through a multidisciplinary team with surgical and nonsurgical expertise in selection, implantation, and follow-up; provide on-call complication cover, urgent neurosurgical or spinal referral arrangements, adequate caseloads, professional development, peer review, and outcome assessment.
recommendations.rationale: Coordinated expertise supports safe delivery and management of complications.
recommendations.source_heading: Appropriate Context for Delivery: A Sociopsychobiomedical Model

recommendations.statement: Include comprehensive psychiatric and social assessment in candidate evaluation, and address unstable psychiatric conditions, poor coping, or unresolved social issues before proceeding.
recommendations.rationale: These factors can adversely affect adherence and SCS outcomes.
recommendations.source_heading: Appropriate Context for Delivery: A Sociopsychobiomedical Model

recommendations.statement: Recommend smoking cessation, weight loss, and physical therapy when appropriate before neurostimulation.
recommendations.rationale: Smoking, excess weight, and poor conditioning can impair outcomes and increase procedural or healing risks; preoperative protocols require further research.
recommendations.source_heading: Appropriate Context for Delivery: A Sociopsychobiomedical Model

recommendations.statement: Use trial success—>50% pain reduction on the numeric rating scale or visual analog scale together with better function—as a principal predictor when considering permanent SCS implantation. Also assess patient-reported quality of life and daily activities, and evaluate functional gains independently.
recommendations.rationale: Pain and function together provide a broader assessment of likely long-term benefit.

recommendations.statement: Conduct SCS trials for five to seven days in general, adapting duration to the patient's needs while considering safety; trials >ten days increase complication risk without adding predictive value.
recommendations.rationale: Longer trials increase complications, especially infection.

recommendations.statement: Generally follow a trial-first approach. In suitable patients, particularly when multidisciplinary assessment strongly favors benefit, SCS implantation may instead proceed without a prior trial if the implanter has an implant-to-trial ratio >80% and has performed >100 implants.
recommendations.rationale: The cited TRIAL-STIM study found no significant difference in long-term outcomes between the approaches.

recommendations.statement: Obtain specialist and multidisciplinary review of conservative-treatment response, pain suitability, and physical, psychologic, and social factors; optimize glucose and smoking status, manage anticoagulants, and choose the IPG according to anatomy and preferences, including charging options and MRI compatibility.
Educate patients and caregivers about the purpose, benefits, risks, trial, equipment, need for active participation, realistic expectations, and the usually gradual course of improvement.

Assess active or insufficiently managed depression, anxiety, and other psychologic difficulties, including pain catastrophizing, and recommend interventions such as cognitive behavioral therapy where appropriate.
recommendations.rationale: Psychologic difficulties may worsen outcomes and adherence.

recommendations.statement: Use MRI to assess epidural anatomy and plan the approach for lead placement.

Give a first-generation cephalosporin, such as cefazolin, within 30–60 min before incision; consult a local infectious disease specialist for β-lactam allergies, repeat antibiotics during procedures >2 h or with significant blood loss, and avoid continuing prophylaxis beyond 24 h postoperatively.
recommendations.rationale: These measures aim to prevent surgical-site infection.

recommendations.statement: Manage anticoagulant interruption according to half-life and bleeding risk: stop warfarin 5 d before surgery and verify the international normalized ratio before the procedure; stop clopidogrel 7 d beforehand and allow 5 half-lives for newer anticoagulants. Resume anticoagulants 24 h after the procedure unless contraindicated.

Screen SCS trial and implantation candidates for S aureus colonization, including methicillin-resistant S aureus. For carriers, use nasal mupirocin 2% ointment and daily chlorhexidine gluconate body washes for 5 d before the procedure; seek infectious disease advice for MRSA colonization, resistance, or relevant allergies.
recommendations.rationale: Decolonization has been shown to reduce surgical-site infection, particularly deep infection involving implants.
recommendations.source_heading: Preoperative Staphylococcus aureus Screening and Decolonization

recommendations.statement: Choose paddle leads when greater stability is required or percutaneous access is unsuitable; have a trained neurosurgeon place them using preoperative MRI planning, meticulous technique, and appropriate anchoring.
recommendations.rationale: Paddle leads can improve efficacy and reduce migration in appropriate cases, although percutaneous leads have fewer complications and revisions.

recommendations.statement: Prepare skin with an antiseptic such as chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine and allow it to dry adequately.
recommendations.rationale: Skin antisepsis reduces infection risk.

recommendations.statement: Keep sedation as light as feasible while maintaining comfort and limiting movement; consider deeper sedation or full anesthesia according to patient and procedural factors. Use intraoperative neuromonitoring when difficult cervical lead placement is anticipated, but not routinely for T12 entry.
Maintain strict asepsis, including hand hygiene, sterile equipment, frequent glove changes, and reduced operating-room traffic.
recommendations.rationale: These measures reduce infection risk.

recommendations.statement: Position patients appropriately and use fluoroscopy for accurate epidural lead placement; secure leads with mechanical or suture anchors, handle tissues carefully, maintain hemostasis, minimize dead space, and avoid positioning device edges beneath incision lines.
recommendations.rationale: Accurate placement and anchoring support stimulation coverage and limit migration and surgical complications.

recommendations.statement: Close wounds with accurate edge approximation, limited tension, and elimination of dead space; irrigate with saline. Antimicrobial irrigation may be considered for high-risk patients, but do not use chlorhexidine- or alcohol-containing solutions for irrigation. Consider iodophor-impregnated drapes in high-risk cases, apply an occlusive postoperative dressing, and teach wound care.
recommendations.rationale: Appropriate closure and wound care reduce complications; antiseptic wound dressings remain controversial.

recommendations.statement: Before surgery, treat infections elsewhere, optimize glucose control, stop tobacco use, decolonize S aureus carriers with mupirocin and chlorhexidine baths, and give timely weight-based antibiotic prophylaxis. Perform a surgical scrub for 2–5 min, avoid artificial nails, and use clippers for hair removal.
recommendations.rationale: NSANZ endorses these infection-management practices while recognizing that evidence is extrapolated from other surgical settings.

recommendations.statement: During surgery, wear a mask, cap, sterile gown, and gloves, with double gloving recommended; use chlorhexidine skin antisepsis and iodophor-impregnated drapes. Limit room traffic and operative time, maintain hemostasis, avoid dead space, use laminar flow with high-efficiency particulate air filtration, and irrigate with saline before closure.
recommendations.rationale: NSANZ endorses these practices while acknowledging extrapolation from other surgical settings.

recommendations.statement: After surgery, keep an occlusive dressing for 24–48 h and avoid antibiotics for >24 h. Teach wound care, symptoms of surgical-site infection, and hand hygiene during dressing changes; treat suspected infection with antibiotics selected using local resistance patterns and culture results.
recommendations.rationale: NSANZ endorses these practices while acknowledging extrapolation from other surgical settings.

recommendations.statement: Use cefazolin as first-line surgical antibiotic prophylaxis. If resistance requires another agent, consider clindamycin, vancomycin, or teicoplanin according to local resistance and infectious disease advice; administer antibiotics within 60 minutes before incision, or 120 minutes beforehand when vancomycin is used alone.
recommendations.context: Choice and timing of prophylactic antibiotic
recommendations.rationale: S aureus and S epidermidis are the principal pathogens associated with SCS infection.

recommendations.statement: Assess anticoagulated or antiplatelet-treated patients and patients with coagulopathy individually. Interrupt anticoagulants for 5 half-lives; reserve bridging for patients at high clotting risk after advice from their hematologist, cardiologist, or neurologist. Stop supplements affecting coagulation and obtain preoperative neuraxial MRI or computed tomography for altered coagulation.
recommendations.rationale: SCS lead placement and removal carry moderate-to-high bleeding risk, including epidural hematoma.

recommendations.statement: Stop aspirin used for primary prophylaxis 6 d before SCS. For secondary prophylaxis, use shared decision-making to balance cardiovascular and procedural risks. Stop nonaspirin nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs for 5 half-lives before the procedure.
Monitor for bleeding during and after SCS procedures. Resume anticoagulants 24 h after the procedure in low-risk cases and 48 h afterward in high-risk cases.
Recognize suspected epidural hematoma promptly, confirm it with MRI, and arrange timely surgical decompression, ideally within 24 hours of symptom onset.
recommendations.rationale: Delay can result in permanent neurologic injury.

recommendations.statement: When deep infection is suspected after SCS, use blood tests and imaging such as computed tomography or MRI to establish its presence and identify complications, including epidural abscess.
recommendations.rationale: Physical examination alone may not reliably distinguish superficial from deep infection.

recommendations.statement: When infection necessitates device removal, wait a minimum of 12 weeks before reimplantation to allow complete resolution, then place the new device on the contralateral side.
recommendations.rationale: Contralateral placement aims to limit recurrence.

recommendations.statement: Treat superficial postimplantation infection with oral antibiotics for 7–10 d; device removal is generally unnecessary unless treatment fails.

For deep postimplantation infection, remove the device, surgically debride infected tissue, and give extended culture-guided antibiotics. Intervene urgently for epidural abscess or meningitis and involve an infectious disease specialist.

Provide structured inpatient and outpatient follow-up after SCS trials and permanent implantation, with urgent review available for time-critical complications. Maintain daily follow-up and direct patient–clinician contact throughout a trial.
recommendations.rationale: Prompt review permits detection of complications such as epidural hematoma, dural puncture headache, and lead migration.

recommendations.statement: Inspect wounds for infection, hematoma, and impaired healing; arrange an initial review within 1–2 wk and further assessment as needed. Teach patients infection warning signs and when to seek care.
recommendations.rationale: Surgical wound infections often become apparent after 5 d.

recommendations.statement: Review programming and device function after implantation, with sessions suggested at 2–4 wk, 3 mo, 6 mo, and 12 mo and extra visits when needed. For possible hypersensitivity to paresthesia-free stimulation, consider graduated amplitude adjustment and intermittent dosing. Remote programming may be used when Wi-Fi is stable, at clinician discretion.
recommendations.rationale: Adjustments may help sustain benefit and address overstimulation-related pain in a minority of patients.

recommendations.statement: Maintain protocols to detect and manage infection, lead migration, device malfunction, and neurologic symptoms; ensure access to imaging and give patients clear instructions for urgent contact. Reinforce wound care, activity restrictions, device operation, and regular follow-up.

Use multimodal rehabilitation after SCS, combining physical therapy for safe movement and motor control with cognitive-behavioral techniques; counsel patients about gradual activity resumption and device-related risks.
recommendations.rationale: The approach aims to improve function, although direct high-quality comparisons with standard postoperative care and formal expert consensus are lacking.
recommendations.source_heading: Physical Therapy and Movement After SCS

recommendations.statement: Collect standardized SCS outcome data across centers for a registry, including patient characteristics, device and programming details, surgical information, clinical outcomes, revisions, explantations, and complications; assess effectiveness at 6 mo and annually.
recommendations.rationale: Consistent reporting supports comparison and quality improvement.
recommendations.source_heading: Defining Outcome Measures for an SCS Registry

recommendations.statement: Systematically collect and review SCS service data, compare results with national and international registries, hold regular interdisciplinary morbidity and mortality reviews, and monitor postmarket device safety and performance.
recommendations.rationale: Ongoing review can identify complications and opportunities to improve selection, procedures, and programming.
recommendations.source_heading: Audit and Quality Improvement for SCS

recommendations.statement: Give patients with SCS clear emergency instructions, including how to contact their provider or obtain urgent care for severe pain or complications, and arrange follow-up after an emergency.
recommendations.rationale: Prompt access and review support management of serious complications.

recommendations.statement: Provide structured mentorship before clinicians independently perform SCS, covering patient-centered and culturally sensitive care, selection, anatomy, imaging, implantation, devices, troubleshooting, complications, and postimplantation management.
recommendations.rationale: Supervised competency development supports safe practice.

recommendations.statement: Limit SCS procedures to appropriately trained clinicians and clinical settings that meet sound medical, professional, and ethical standards, except for ethically approved research involving emerging indications or new devices. Maintain accreditation, liability insurance, continuing education, skills, peer evaluation, and outcome audits.
recommendations.rationale: Inadequate training and failure to review practice can undermine patient safety.

recommendations.statement: Practice within professional competence and applicable Australian or New Zealand legal and ethical requirements; document accurately and communicate benefits, harms, risks, and alternatives clearly and without bias to support shared decisions.
recommendations.rationale: Failure to meet these obligations can have patient-safety and medico-legal consequences.

recommendations.statement: Comply with device postmarket requirements, including safety surveillance, adverse-event reporting, and periodic renewals.
recommendations.rationale: Ongoing oversight supports device safety and reliability.
recommendations.source_heading: Use of Newer Devices on the Market

artifacts.title: Table 6. Patient Preparation for SCS

rows: Specialist consultation

Assess response to conservative treatment and suitability of the pain type for neuromodulation. A multidisciplinary team review is recommended to examine physical, psychologic, and social influences on outcomes. Optimize glucose control, support smoking cessation, and manage anticoagulants under clinical guidelines. Select IPGs according to anatomy and preferences, including rechargeable status and MRI compatibility.
Patient/caregiver education

Explain the treatment process, purpose, possible benefits and risks, trial expectations, and equipment use. Address realistic expectations, the need for active participation, and the usually gradual course of improvement.
Timing of SCS implantation
Studies generally associate earlier implantation in the course of chronic pain with greater SCS efficacy.
Psychologic evaluation

Assess active or insufficiently managed conditions such as depression or anxiety. Identify "yellow flags," including pain catastrophizing, and recommend interventions such as cognitive behavioral therapy to improve readiness and adherence.
Diagnostic imaging
Use MRI to assess epidural anatomy and plan the approach for lead placement.
Antibiotic prophylaxis

Give a first-generation cephalosporin, such as cefazolin, within 30–60 min before incision. For β-lactam allergies, consult a local infectious disease specialist. Avoid antibiotic treatment beyond 24 h postoperatively; repeat dosing for procedures >2 h or substantial blood loss.
Management of anticoagulation

Stop anticoagulants according to half-life and bleeding risk. Stop warfarin 5 d before surgery and verify the international normalized ratio before the procedure; stop clopidogrel 7 d beforehand and allow 5 half-lives for newer anticoagulants. Resume anticoagulants 24 h after the procedure unless contraindicated.
Infection screening and decolonization

Obtain a nasal swab for S aureus, including methicillin-resistant strains. For carriers, use nasal mupirocin 2% ointment and daily chlorhexidine gluconate body washes for 5 d before the procedure to reduce surgical-site infections. Seek local infectious disease advice for MRSA colonization.

artifacts.summary: The table organizes consultations, education, assessment, imaging, prophylaxis, and anticoagulation management before SCS.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It provides a preparation checklist addressing treatment suitability and preventable procedural risks.

artifacts.title: Table 7. Surgical Techniques and Best Practices for SCS

rows: Skin preparation
Apply an antiseptic such as chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine and allow sufficient drying time to lower infection risk.
Anesthetic management

Keep sedation as light as feasible for comfort and reduced movement; consider deeper sedation or full anesthesia according to patient and procedure. Intraoperative neuromonitoring is recommended for anticipated difficulty with cervical leads, but is not routinely needed for T12 entry.
Aseptic technique
Maintain strict sterile practice, change gloves frequently, and require hand hygiene and aseptic conduct from all surgical staff.
Incision and pocket creation
Follow tissue planes for access and create a subcutaneous generator pocket with minimal tissue disruption.
Lead placement
Position leads with fluoroscopic guidance to optimize coverage; position the patient to facilitate epidural access and avoid pressure injury.
Anchoring
Use mechanical or suture anchors to stabilize leads and reduce migration.
Tissue handling
Dissect carefully to limit trauma, achieve hemostasis with bipolar electrocautery, and keep device edges away from incision lines.
Surgical instruments and anchor
Use instruments appropriately and favor minimal access. Limit excessive electrocautery, eliminate dead space, and anchor leads securely.
Infection control measures
Use sterile equipment, hand hygiene, and reduced operating-room traffic. Preoperative chlorhexidine and alcohol-based skin preparation lowers infection risk.
Wound closure and dressing

Approximate wound edges precisely while removing dead space and limiting tension. Saline irrigation is recommended. Antimicrobial irrigation may be considered for high-risk patients, but chlorhexidine- or alcohol-containing solutions should not be used. Sutures and skin adhesives may form a microbial barrier; consider iodophor-impregnated drapes for high-risk cases. Apply an occlusive postoperative dressing and teach wound care. Antiseptic wound dressings remain controversial.
Immediate response to complications

Arrange regular device and complication reviews. Ensure a skilled multidisciplinary team can address respiratory, cardiovascular, or neurologic events, with emergency imaging and urgent neurosurgical or spinal referral pathways available.

rows: Risk stratification

Assess anticoagulant or antiplatelet use and coagulopathy individually. Stop anticoagulants for 5 half-lives, including novel oral anticoagulants. Reserve bridging for patients at high clotting risk, with hematologist, cardiologist, or neurologist advice. Stop supplements affecting coagulation, including fish oil, garlic, and gingko biloba. For altered coagulation, obtain preoperative neuraxial MRI or computed tomography to reduce epidural hematoma risk.
Timing

Stop aspirin used for primary prophylaxis 6 d before the procedure. For secondary prophylaxis, weigh cardiovascular and procedural risks through shared decision-making. Stop nonaspirin nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs for 5 half-lives before SCS.
Intra- and postoperative monitoring
During and after SCS, watch for bleeding signs, including hematoma formation.

Resume anticoagulants 24 h after the procedure in low-risk cases and 48 h after it in high-risk cases.
