artifacts.title: Table 10. Early Complications in SCS

rows: Neurologic injury

Occurs in 0.1%–2.3% of cases. Potential causes are direct injury, bleeding-related neural compression, and impaired blood supply causing ischemia. Complex anatomy, obesity, and repeat procedures increase risk; shallow needle angles and oblique fluoroscopic views may reduce it.
Vascular injury

Rare with midline SCS, including injury to the artery of Adamkiewicz. Risk is greater with DRG stimulation because of possible mechanical impingement; neurologic complication rates reported for DRG stimulation range from 0%–8.8%.
Bleeding and hematoma

Minor bleeding is common. Major bleeding may produce an epidural hematoma requiring urgent imaging and decompression within 24 h. Anticoagulants and supplements increase bleeding risk; a pocket hematoma may require surgical evacuation.
Dural breach and cerebrospinal fluid leak

Dural breach occurs in 0.2%–2% of cases, often with spinal stenosis, adhesions, or obesity. Cerebrospinal fluid leakage and spinal headache usually resolve with conservative care; refractory cases may require an epidural blood patch.
Anesthesia-related complications
General anesthesia is rarely used in Australia and New Zealand but may cause hemodynamic instability, especially with severe comorbidity. Careful preoperative planning can reduce risk.

artifacts.summary: The table describes early neurologic, vascular, bleeding, dural, and anesthesia-related complications, including reported rates and responses.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It supports early recognition and urgent action when complications threaten neurologic function.

artifacts.title: Table 11. Common Delayed Complications in SCS

rows: Infection

Occurs in 2%–4% of cases and may be superficial, deep, or epidural. Risk factors include diabetes, immunosuppression, smoking, prolonged trials, high opioid doses, and S aureus colonization; hospitalization before surgery increases risk fourfold. Presentation is usually ≥3 d after surgery, with inflammation, excessive pain, purulent discharge, or fever. Inflammatory markers may be raised but can be absent. Early recognition and prevention are important; superficial infection may respond to antibiotics, whereas deeper infection often requires device removal.
Pocket pain and seroma

Persistent IPG pocket pain affects 5%–20% of cases and is often related to battery size or location. Topical anesthetics may help; severe cases may require surgical relocation. Seromas or hygromas may be managed with aspiration and a binder.
Lead migration
Occurs in 2%–10% of cases, usually because of inadequate anchoring. It reduces efficacy without posing a neurologic threat; lead repositioning may restore function.
Other device-related issues
Include hardware malfunction, battery failure, uncommon allergic reactions, and lead adhesions that may diminish stimulation delivery over time.

artifacts.summary: The table identifies delayed infections, pocket problems, lead migration, and other hardware issues, with their consequences and management.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It helps interpret loss of benefit or new symptoms after implantation and choose an appropriate response.

artifacts.title: Table 12. Characteristics and Management of Postimplantation Infections in SCS

rows: Superficial infections
First 7–14 d postimplantation
Limited to skin and subcutaneous tissue, with possible incision-site redness, pain, swelling, and drainage.
Treat with oral antibiotics for 7–10 d. Removal of the device is usually unnecessary unless treatment fails.
Deep infections
Within 90 d postimplantation

Affect deeper soft tissue, muscle, fascia, and the SCS device; possible consequences include epidural abscess, osteomyelitis, or meningitis. Wound separation, purulent drainage, or device erosion may occur.

Remove the device, debride surgically, and give extended antibiotics directed by cultures. Epidural abscess or meningitis requires urgent intervention; infectious disease specialist involvement is recommended.

artifacts.summary: The table contrasts superficial and deep infection by timing, tissue involvement, signs, and treatment.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The distinction informs whether antibiotics alone may suffice or urgent intervention and device removal are required.

artifacts.title: Table 13. Key Components of Posttrial and Postimplantation Monitoring for SCS

rows: Posttrial and postimplantation monitoring

Trials may take place in day surgery or with overnight admission, but urgent assessment must be available for time-critical events such as epidural hematoma. During the trial, daily follow-up and direct patient–clinician communication are essential for detecting complications such as dural puncture headache or lead migration.
Wound surveillance

Check surgical wounds for infection, hematoma, and impaired healing. An initial review within 1–2 wk is recommended, followed by further assessments as needed. Teach infection warning signs and when to seek care because wound infections often appear after 5 d.
Programming and device management

Programming often needs repeated adjustment after implantation; visits are suggested at 2–4 wk, 3 mo, 6 mo, and 12 mo. In a minority of patients, hypersensitivity to paresthesia-free waveforms and relative overstimulation over time may provoke pain. Graduated amplitude adjustment and intermittent dosing may mitigate this; additional visits may be needed. Remote programming may be used when Wi-Fi is stable, subject to clinician judgment.
Monitoring for complications

Maintain protocols for identifying and managing infection, lead migration, hardware malfunction, and neurologic symptoms. Provide access to imaging for complication assessment and clear instructions for urgent contact with the healthcare team.
Patient/caregiver education
Repeat guidance on wound care, activity limits, operating the device and remote control, adherence to postoperative instructions, and regular follow-up.

artifacts.summary: The table specifies surveillance, programming, complication monitoring, and education after SCS trials and implantation.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It supports timely detection of complications and adjustments needed to sustain therapeutic benefit.

artifacts.title: Table 14. Comprehensive Outcome Measures for SCS Therapy
artifacts.source_heading: Standard and Quality Improvement Defining Outcome Measures for an SCS Registry

rows: Patient demographics
Record age, sex, comorbidities, and baseline health to contextualize individual outcomes.
Device information
Record stimulator brand, model, type, and programming settings, including pulse width and frequency.
Surgical details
Document the operative approach, perioperative complications, and adverse events during surgery.
Clinical outcomes

Capture pain reduction before and after implantation, including numeric rating scale results; medication reduction, including Medication Quantification Scale; function, including Oswestry Disability Index and activity tolerance; and quality of life, including EQ-5D and Patient Global Impression of Change. Evaluate effectiveness at 6 mo and annually.
Revision and complications

Track revision indications and timing, device survival, and complications such as infection and lead migration. Record explantation events, reasons including battery change, malfunction, or inadequate pain relief, and device performance. Current registry data report a 7.6% explantation rate over 3 y.

artifacts.summary: The table defines patient, device, procedure, outcome, and revision data for standardized SCS reporting.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Consistent measures allow outcome assessment, complication surveillance, and comparison across services.

artifacts.title: Table 15. Key Quality Improvement Strategies for SCS Therapy
artifacts.source_heading: Audit and Quality Improvement for SCS

rows: Data collection and benchmarking

Units should routinely gather and analyze key measures and compare them with national and international SCS registries. This can reveal trends, complications, and opportunities to improve surgery, selection, and programming.
Interdisciplinary review
Hold regular morbidity and mortality meetings so different disciplines can examine outcomes and complications and improve practice.
Outcome monitoring
Review collected outcomes continuously to maintain care standards. Use postmarket real-world information to assess device safety and performance, inform patient decisions, and refine treatment.

artifacts.summary: The table presents data benchmarking, interdisciplinary case review, and ongoing outcome monitoring as quality-improvement strategies.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: These activities help services identify safety concerns and refine SCS care using observed outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Objectives
document_sections.content: The Neuromodulation Society of Australia and New Zealand (NSANZ) developed evidence-based guidance on spinal cord stimulation (SCS) for chronic pain. Its main aim is to support evidence-informed care in Australia and New Zealand, particularly in patient selection, procedural practice, and complication management.

document_sections.heading: Materials and Methods
document_sections.content: A systematic review searched Medline, EMBASE, Trip Pro, and Google Scholar for publications from 2010 to July 2024. The guideline included 283 studies and relevant clinical guidelines selected for level 1B evidence or strong expert consensus consistent with Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation criteria. Clinical questions followed the Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome framework. NSANZ board members used a Delphi process to reach consensus.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: The guidance addresses patient selection and preparation, procedural methods, care after implantation, and complications. It also covers training, quality improvement, and multidisciplinary cooperation. Its principal recommendations seek better selection, safer procedures, and improved outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The guidance offers practical, evidence-informed advice for safe and effective SCS in chronic pain. It aims to make care more consistent, transparent, and collaborative across Australia and New Zealand.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: Neuromodulation can relieve chronic pain when conventional treatments have not provided adequate options. Greater variation and complexity in devices, techniques, and patient groups create a need for standardized care that supports safety, effectiveness, and equitable access. SCS shows promise for neuropathic and other difficult chronic pain, but differences in selection, procedures, and care after implantation contribute to inconsistent results. NSANZ developed this guidance to improve outcomes and reduce complications through recommendations on selection, procedures, training, and complication management. Deep brain stimulation and sacral nerve stimulation fall outside its scope. A shared SCS framework is intended to support consistent care across clinical settings, collaboration, innovation, and research.

document_sections.heading: MATERIALS AND METHODS
document_sections.content: Guideline development drew on a systematic review of SCS literature and a consensus process.

document_sections.heading: Search Strategy
document_sections.content: A medical librarian helped design searches of Medline through OVID, EMBASE, Trip Pro, and Google Scholar. Searches combined terms concerning spinal cord stimulation, indications, complications, efficacy, and guidelines, using Boolean operators, wildcards, and MeSH terms. Eligible publication years ran from 2010 to 2024; the search was updated on July 12, 2024. No language restriction applied. The record-identification flowchart reports n = 1201 records from Medline, n = 1,201 screened, n = 918 excluded, n = 283 sought for retrieval, n = 283 assessed for eligibility, and n=283 included. It marks registered records, prescreening removals, records not retrieved, and exclusions after eligibility assessment as n/a.

document_sections.heading: Selection Process
document_sections.content: Two reviewers independently examined titles and abstracts, and a third resolved disagreements. Potentially eligible studies underwent full-text review. The search identified 1201 citations; screening left 283 included studies. Manual searching identified further guidelines. The selection process was summarized using standard methods.

document_sections.heading: Eligibility Criteria
document_sections.content: Included studies supplied at least level 1B evidence, described as randomized controlled trials [RCTs] with narrow confidence intervals, or strong expert-consensus recommendations consistent with Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations criteria. Position statements from recognized bodies, including the Australia and New Zealand Faculty of Medicine, were also considered.

document_sections.heading: Data Extraction and Analysis
document_sections.content: The developers framed key questions using the Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome framework and synthesized extracted data into recommendations. The NSANZ board used a Delphi process to resolve conflicting recommendations.

document_sections.heading: NSANZ Recommendations for Best Practice Patient Selection
document_sections.content: This part addresses which pain phenotypes and clinical circumstances warrant consideration of SCS, as well as contraindications and individualized decisions.

document_sections.heading: Pain Phenotypes Suitable for Neuromodulation
document_sections.content: NSANZ recommends SCS for appropriately selected people with refractory neuropathic or mixed pain who have not obtained adequate pain relief or functional improvement despite comprehensive multidisciplinary management. Table 1 compares pain phenotypes, applicable conditions, and the strength or limitations of their supporting evidence.

document_sections.heading: Indications
document_sections.content: SCS is recommended for chronic, refractory pain that has not responded to standard medical treatment. Careful selection and compliance with the specified criteria are important for better outcomes. Table 2 summarizes indications and their evidence, including PSPS, CRPS, PDN, peripheral vascular disease, refractory angina, and emerging uses.

document_sections.heading: Contraindications
document_sections.content: SCS is contraindicated when its potential harms exceed its potential benefits. NSANZ emphasizes assessment tailored to the individual, interdisciplinary advice, and shared decisions to address modifiable risks. Table 3 distinguishes absolute from relative contraindications.

document_sections.heading: Target and SCS/Peripheral Nerve Stimulation Modality Selection
document_sections.content: The choice of stimulation target and modality should account for the patient's pain mechanism, anatomy, likely benefit, and procedural risk.

document_sections.heading: Targets for SCS and Peripheral Nerve Stimulation
document_sections.content: Potential SCS targets extend along the accessible spinal cord from C2 to the conus and depend on whether the pain mechanism is neuropathic or nociplastic. NSANZ emphasizes tailoring the target to improve benefit while limiting risk. Table 4 relates stimulation regions and modalities to studied conditions and the available evidence.

document_sections.heading: Pain Phenotype, Indication, and Stimulation Target with Limited Evidence
document_sections.content: NSANZ recognizes that strong evidence is lacking for some phenotypes, indications, and targets. Treatment in those circumstances may be considered using expert judgment, multidisciplinary input, clinical need, the absence of viable alternatives, and comprehensive informed consent. The clinical record should clearly explain the reasoning about benefits and risks to support transparent, patient-centered shared decisions.

document_sections.heading: Cervical Neurostimulation
document_sections.content: NSANZ supports cervical SCS in carefully selected patients with cervical radicular pain, upper-extremity CRPS, cervical axial pain, or persistent spinal pain syndrome (cervical), on evidence suggesting moderate benefit. Imaging and precise surgery should guide optimal lead placement between C2 and C6. NSANZ supports epidural access at C7–T4 or T11–L1 for safe navigation toward cervical targets, with attention to anatomy. Practitioners must undertake accredited workshops and supervised training; proficiency in thoracic neuromodulation is advised before cervical cases. A minimum of ten SCS or dorsal root ganglion (DRG) procedures annually is recommended to maintain expertise. Continuing education and peer review are important for safety and outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Stimulation Modes
document_sections.content: SCS modes differ in their mechanisms and possible clinical benefits, as outlined in Table 5. The Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) calls for more research to establish the efficacy of newer waveforms because the existing evidence varies. NSANZ emphasizes choosing a mode for the individual's pain phenotype and anatomy: responses differ, and evidence for newer modes remains emerging.

document_sections.heading: DRG Stimulation
document_sections.content: NSANZ recommends DRG stimulation as an advanced option for focal neuropathic pain, especially CRPS and persistent spinal pain syndrome (PSPS). Some evidence suggests better efficacy than traditional SCS for focal neuropathic pain, with benefits sustained long term. Specific risks include implantable pulse generator (IPG) site pain, lead migration or fracture, infection, and greater vascular and neurologic injury risk at cervical and thoracic placements. Selection and procedural planning should minimize those risks. NSANZ emphasizes accredited fellowships, practical workshops, and supervised experience. Only clinicians with recognized DRG expertise should place leads above T10, up to a maximum of the C6 level; these procedures should have multidisciplinary support, comprehensive informed consent, and documented clinical and risk–benefit reasoning.

document_sections.heading: Timing and Context of Delivery Duration of Conservative Management Before Neurostimulation
document_sections.content: Before considering neurostimulation, NSANZ recommends a multimodal conservative-treatment trial within multidisciplinary care, typically six to 12 months, adjusted to the condition and response. This helps identify truly refractory patients likely to benefit. Continuing ineffective conservative care too long may postpone useful intervention, particularly in PSPS and CRPS, for which earlier neurostimulation can lessen pain and opioid use. Although noninvasive care helps some patients, timely neurostimulation should be considered for refractory pain to improve outcomes and limit opioid dependence.

document_sections.heading: Patient Engagement and Neurostimulation Outcomes
document_sections.content: NSANZ stresses active patient participation. Candidates should have adequate cognition, realistic expectations, and motivation for rehabilitation after implantation. Patients who cannot engage actively, including those with substantial cognitive impairment, should not receive an implant. Attendance at follow-up, adherence to prescribed care, and psychosocial support help outcomes and complication management; a strong support network also promotes engagement and success.

document_sections.heading: Opioid Rationalization and SCS Implantation
document_sections.content: For chronic noncancer pain, NSANZ recommends rationalizing opioid treatment in accordance with Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists (ANZCA) Faculty of Pain Medicine guidance. Before an SCS trial or implant, rotation to the atypical opioids tapentadol and/or buprenorphine is advisable; if opioid intolerant, <90 mg oral morphine equivalent daily dose (OMEDD) is preferred. Evidence supports opioid weaning before implantation to improve long-term results and reduce late device failure. Higher doses are associated with less SCS success, possibly because opioid-induced hyperalgesia impairs efficacy; tapentadol and buprenorphine carry a lower risk of that effect. The study by Nissen et al reports better pain control and fewer failures among patients weaned before implantation. NSANZ recommends combining behavioral therapy, physical rehabilitation, and nonopioid medication to aid tapering, reduce withdrawal symptoms, and prepare for SCS.

document_sections.heading: Appropriate Context for Delivery: A Sociopsychobiomedical Model
document_sections.content: NSANZ recommends multidisciplinary neuromodulation care involving surgical and nonsurgical specialists. Teams need expertise in selection, implantation, and follow-up, an effective on-call service for complications, arrangements for urgent neurosurgical or spinal referral, and sufficient cases to maintain skills. Professional development, peer review, outcome assessment, and effective communication support care quality. Candidate assessment must thoroughly address psychiatric and social circumstances. Stable mental health and sufficient support aid adherence and success; unstable psychiatric illness, ineffective coping, or unresolved social matters such as medical litigation should be addressed first because they adversely affect SCS outcomes. Excess weight, smoking, and poor conditioning may worsen outcomes through infection, lead migration, and impaired wound healing. NSANZ recommends smoking cessation, weight loss, and physical therapy to improve surgical and functional outcomes and reduce complications, particularly in low back pain. More research is needed to establish preoperative protocols incorporating these measures.

document_sections.heading: SCS Trial Predicting Long-Term Success of SCS
document_sections.content: NSANZ recommends using a successful trial as a major predictor of longer-term benefit from permanent SCS. Success is defined by >50% pain reduction on the numeric rating scale or visual analog scale together with improved function. Patient-reported quality of life and daily activities should supplement objective measures; mobility, endurance, and other relevant functional tasks should be assessed separately. Lower initial opioid use and favorable psychosocial factors also predict success. Outcomes are more likely to be better with opioid doses <90 mg OMEDD. NSANZ recommends reducing opioid use before a trial when feasible.

document_sections.heading: Optimal Duration of SCS Trials
document_sections.content: NSANZ recommends trials lasting five to seven days to assess pain and function during ordinary activities. Trials >ten days increase complications, especially infections, without improving prediction. The five-to-seven-day period balances assessment with safety; clinicians should still tailor duration to patient needs while considering efficacy and risk.

document_sections.heading: Trial Vs Direct SCS Implantation
document_sections.content: NSANZ retains a trial-first principle because screening trials have traditionally assessed response. It also acknowledges level 1B evidence from the UK-based TRIAL-STIM study showing no significant difference in long-term outcomes between trial-first and direct implantation. Accordingly, direct implantation may be considered for suitable patients, particularly when multidisciplinary assessment strongly predicts benefit, if the implanter has an implant-to-trial ratio >80% and has performed >100 implants.

document_sections.heading: Patient Preparation
document_sections.content: SCS preparation should consider physical, psychological, and social factors because engagement and adherence matter to outcomes. NSANZ recommends the measures summarized in Table 6: specialist and multidisciplinary review, patient and caregiver education, attention to implantation timing and psychological readiness, diagnostic imaging, antibiotic prophylaxis, anticoagulation management, and infection screening and decolonization.

document_sections.heading: Preoperative Staphylococcus aureus Screening and Decolonization
document_sections.content: Staphylococcus aureus, frequently originating from the patient, is the leading cause of surgical-site infection in orthopedic and neurosurgical procedures. Nasal mupirocin and chlorhexidine bathing protocols have been shown to reduce such infections, particularly deep infections involving implants. NSANZ recommends screening patients undergoing SCS trials or implantation for S aureus carriage, decolonizing carriers, and obtaining infectious-disease advice when resistance to mupirocin or allergy to mupirocin or chlorhexidine requires a tailored approach.

document_sections.heading: Surgical Technique
document_sections.content: Implantation requires careful planning, performance, and follow-up for safety and effectiveness. NSANZ recommends the surgical practices summarized in Table 7, including preparation, anesthesia, asepsis, lead positioning and anchoring, tissue and wound management, infection control, and prompt responses to complications.

document_sections.heading: Procedures
document_sections.content: NSANZ links implantation success to comprehensive planning, accurate lead positioning, secure anchoring, and careful tissue handling. Strict infection prevention and meticulous closure reduce risk. Wound care and regular postoperative reviews contribute to durable results.

document_sections.heading: Surgical Placement of Paddle Lead
document_sections.content: NSANZ recommends paddle leads when greater stability is needed or percutaneous access is unsuitable. Percutaneous leads have fewer complications and require fewer revisions, whereas paddle leads can provide better efficacy and less migration in appropriate cases. Paddle implantation requires advanced skills and should be done by a trained neurosurgeon. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), precise planning, and careful anchoring help limit complications.

document_sections.heading: Surgical Infection and Bleeding Management
document_sections.content: No trials provide level 1 evidence specifically for implanted pain-neuromodulation devices to inform this guidance. Extensive research on surgical-site and implanted-device infections generally, together with level 2 evidence specific to implanted neuromodulatory devices, supports applying general preparatory and prophylactic infection-prevention measures to SCS.

document_sections.heading: Antibiotic Prophylaxis
document_sections.content: S aureus and S epidermidis are the main organisms implicated in SCS infections. Evidence supports cefazolin as first-line surgical prophylaxis. Where resistance warrants an alternative, clindamycin, vancomycin, or teicoplanin may be selected according to local patterns with infectious-disease guidance. Give antibiotics within 60 minutes before incision, or 120 minutes beforehand when vancomycin is used for mono-prophylaxis. NSANZ endorses the Neurostimulation Appropriateness Consensus Committee Recommendations for InfectionManagement Practices in Table 8, while recognizing that evidence from other surgical settings is being applied to epidural leads and SCS IPG placement.

document_sections.heading: Bleeding and Coagulation Management
document_sections.content: SCS has moderate-to-high bleeding risk, especially when placing or removing leads, because of the epidural venous plexuses and large-gauge needles. NSANZ emphasizes anticoagulation management to reduce complications such as epidural hematoma while accounting for patients' cardiovascular needs. Table 9 summarizes perioperative measures. An epidural hematoma is uncommon but serious: early recognition and action are necessary to prevent permanent neurologic injury. MRI should promptly confirm and delineate it; surgical decompression ideally within 24 hours of symptom onset is critical to preserve function.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: Early SCS complications occur during or soon after implantation; delayed complications can appear weeks to months later. Most arise within the first six months following implantation or revision. Hardware problems, including migration and malfunction, are more frequent than biological complications such as infection or dural breach. Complications can substantially harm quality of life and raise healthcare costs, although technological and surgical advances have helped reduce their incidence. NSANZ emphasizes prevention, recognition, and management to protect patients and long-term treatment success.

document_sections.heading: Early Complications
document_sections.content: Early SCS complications are rare but demand vigilance and prompt management. NSANZ emphasizes detailed preoperative planning, appropriate surgical technique, and close postoperative observation to reduce risk. Table 10 summarizes neurologic and vascular injuries, bleeding, dural breach, and anesthesia-related complications.

document_sections.heading: Delayed Complications
document_sections.content: Infection, lead migration, and device problems can undermine long-term SCS outcomes. NSANZ emphasizes prevention, early detection, and effective management to preserve benefit. Table 11 summarizes these delayed complications.

document_sections.heading: Infection Management
document_sections.content: Overall SCS infection rates range from 2% to 4%; deep infection occurs in 1% to 2.5% of cases. NSANZ emphasizes prompt recognition, accurate diagnosis, and treatment; Table 12 distinguishes superficial and deep postimplantation infection. Examination alone may not reliably distinguish them. NSANZ recommends blood tests and imaging such as computed tomography or MRI to confirm deep infection and identify complications including epidural abscess. When device removal is necessary, defer reimplantation for a minimum of 12 weeks to allow infection to resolve fully, and implant the replacement contralaterally to reduce recurrence risk.

document_sections.heading: Long-Term Complications
document_sections.content: Over time, stimulation can become less effective through tolerance, and patients' perception of pain can change. Regular review and reprogramming help maintain benefit. NSANZ emphasizes proactive follow-up, patient and caregiver education, and device adjustment to limit these effects.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up Care
document_sections.content: Structured care after SCS trials and permanent implantation should cover surgical inpatient and outpatient settings and address procedural hazards and complications. Telehealth and remote programming may improve access for rural and interstate patients; referral networks enable shared care. Table 13 summarizes monitoring, wound review, programming, complication response, and education.

document_sections.heading: Physical Therapy and Movement After SCS
document_sections.content: Postimplantation physiotherapy may improve pain, mobility, and quality of life, but no formal expert consensus or high-quality evidence directly compares structured physiotherapy with standard postoperative care. NSANZ recommends multimodal rehabilitation combining physical therapy for safe movement and motor control with cognitive-behavioral approaches. Counseling should support realistic expectations and a gradual return to activity while limiting lead migration and other hardware risks. Only 9.5% to 14% of patients successfully return to work after SCS. Individualized rehabilitation addressing physical and psychosocial needs may improve this outcome. Research including the OPERA RCT is expected to guide post-SCS rehabilitation protocols, particularly for PSPS type 2.

document_sections.heading: Standard and Quality Improvement Defining Outcome Measures for an SCS Registry
document_sections.content: NSANZ recommends standardized SCS outcome measurement so centers can report consistently and support a robust registry. Table 14 sets out patient, device, surgical, clinical-outcome, revision, and complication information to collect.

document_sections.heading: Audit and Quality Improvement for SCS
document_sections.content: NSANZ stresses audits and quality improvement to sustain consistent outcomes, safety, and patient satisfaction. Table 15 describes data collection and benchmarking, interdisciplinary review, and continuous outcome monitoring.

document_sections.heading: Emergency Cover
document_sections.content: NSANZ recommends clear emergency instructions for people with SCS, including how to contact their provider or obtain urgent care for severe pain or complications. Follow-up after an emergency should address problems promptly. Effective management needs experienced multidisciplinary clinicians and access to neurosurgical support for rare serious events. NSANZ aligns with the North American Neuromodulation Society’s curriculum and the ANZCA Faculty of Pain Medicine’s Procedures Endorsement Program, which emphasize safe practice, careful selection, and comprehensive care after procedures. Clear follow-up, wound-care, and maintenance protocols, together with patient participation and team coordination, support safe and durable treatment.

document_sections.heading: Appropriate Training and Mentorship
document_sections.content: NSANZ recommends structured mentorship through fellowship or professional-society involvement before independent SCS practice. Training should cover patient-centered and culturally sensitive care, selection, implantation, devices, and complications, alongside anatomy, imaging, planning, troubleshooting, and postimplantation care. Trainees are encouraged to add society programs, online courses, cadaver workshops, and other training to fellowship experience. Mentored, structured skill development is important for safety and outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Avoiding Poor Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: NSANZ emphasizes compliance with legislation, ethics, and professional standards. SCS clinicians must be appropriately trained, retain accreditation and liability insurance, and continue their education. Inadequate training is a principal cause of poor practice; only clinicians meeting endorsed standards should perform SCS. Breaches of professional or ethical requirements, absence of peer evaluation, failure to maintain surgical skills, and lack of outcome audits threaten safety. Audits should ideally use registries but may review individual practice when no registry exists. NSANZ recommends performing SCS only in settings that maintain sound medical practice, except for ethically approved research trials of emerging indications or new devices.

document_sections.heading: Ethical and Legal Considerations
document_sections.content: NSANZ emphasizes that practitioners in Australia and New Zealand must follow the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency Code of Conduct for Doctors and Medical Council of New Zealand Good Medical Practice. They should work within their competence, maintain the skills needed for safe care, and weigh benefits against harms using evidence-informed decisions. Accurate records, clear and unbiased communication, disclosure of risks and alternatives, and patient-centered shared decisions are essential. SCS practitioners need adequate training and should communicate effectively with patients, primary care providers, and support networks, welcome peer assessment, and seek further supervision or training when needed. Practice must meet accepted professional standards and applicable law. Failure to meet professional or regulatory duties can have medico-legal consequences, particularly for consent, selection, and postprocedural care.

document_sections.heading: Use of Newer Devices on the Market
document_sections.content: The TGA regulates SCS devices as class III (High Risk). They must satisfy the Essential Principles for Safety and Performance, including manufacturing, clinical-evaluation, and performance requirements. Postmarket responsibilities include safety surveillance, adverse-event reporting, and periodic renewals. NSANZ supports these requirements to maintain device safety and reliability throughout use.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: NSANZ's evidence-based guidance seeks more consistent neuromodulation practice through patient selection, training, procedural care, and follow-up. It provides a basis for improving outcomes and meeting patient needs across Australia and New Zealand.
